processing: Scented by the traditional yinzhi method used for Chinese flower teas: base tea is layered with fresh, fragrant blossoms so it takes up their aroma. Specific ratios for this tea are not well documented.
harvest_season: Not well documented. Base tea and blossoms have separate seasons, and as with other scented teas, the scenting happens when the flowers open.
appearance_dry: Like other scented green teas, twisted green leaf, sometimes with a few dried blossoms mixed in.
appearance_liquor: Typical of scented greens: yellow-green and clear.
appearance_wet: Typical of scented greens: soft green leaf, with any blossoms left in the blend.
taste_profile: Expect a citrus-blossom perfume over a green tea base; detailed tasting records for this tea are few.

brewing.notes: General advice for scented green tea: a lidded cup holds the aroma, and water that is too hot flattens both flower and leaf.

vintage_note: As is usual for scented green teas, it is sold by current production and drunk fresh, within a year or so. Scent fades with storage, so it is not a tea to age; keep it sealed and away from other smells.
description:
Daidai huacha is a Chinese flower tea scented with daidai, a sour orange blossom. It is one of the named scented types in Chinese classifications, alongside jasmine, magnolia, osmanthus and zhulan, but far less common than jasmine, which dominates flower tea output.

Flower teas of this kind are made by layering base tea with fresh blossoms so that the dry leaf absorbs their fragrance. Base teas for Chinese flower teas can be green, black, white or oolong; the form described here is the green-based one.

Exact tasting notes for this particular tea are scarce. Going by its flower and base, look for a citrus-blossom aroma on top of a mild green tea. Brew it like a scented green, in a lidded cup with water around 85 C and short steeps.

On the market you may also meet plain dried daidai buds sold as an infusion, which is a different thing with no tea leaf. Check the ingredients if you want real scented tea.
history: The tea is listed by name among the traditional Chinese scented types, but little is documented about where and when it was first made or who made it known.
